Official Week 8 Objectives

1. Describe primary clinical features, CSF findings, and complications of herpesvirus infections in normal and immunocompromised hosts.
2. Explain treatment and prevention strategies, including medications and VZV vaccines.
3. Distinguish herpesviral disease from other pathogens using CSF analysis.
4. Discuss U.S. epidemiology, clinical manifestations, diagnostic tests, and prevention of Mpox.

Slides 2-9: Herpesvirus Family Logic

Slide 5. Herpesviruses are large dsDNA viruses with envelope, tegument, nucleocapsid, and inner DNA core. Surface/tegument glycoproteins mediate entry and replication.
Family identity
Herpes = enveloped dsDNA + latency + reactivation. The envelope makes herpesvirus fragile outside the body.
Slide 8. Alpha = HSV-1/2, VZV; Beta = CMV, HHV-6/7; Gamma = EBV, HHV-8. The current deck emphasizes latency and reactivation across the family.
SubfamilyMembersClinical memory
AlphaHSV-1, HSV-2, VZVNeurotropic latency / recurrent mucocutaneous disease
BetaCMV, HHV-6, HHV-7Congenital/opportunistic CMV; roseola syndromes
GammaEBV, HHV-8Lymphoid latency / oncogenic associations
Handout-only enrichment: the 2029 handout adds that herpesviruses have linear dsDNA, an icosahedral capsid, and nuclear replication. It also gives the classic latency sites: HSV-1 trigeminal ganglia, HSV-2 sacral ganglia, VZV dorsal-root ganglia, EBV B cells, and CMV mononuclear cells.

Slides 10-11: General Laboratory Diagnosis

Slide 10. The deck lists culture, antigen detection, PCR from blood/CSF/other fluids, serology, histopathology/immunohistochemistry, and Tzanck cytopathology.
Slide 11. Tzanck preparation demonstrates multinucleated giant cells. Useful morphologic clue, but not virus-specific.
MethodDeck use
PCR / nucleic acid detectionIdentify herpesviral DNA in blood, CSF, or other body fluids; especially important for HSV encephalitis
SerologyIgM suggests acute infection; IgG prior exposure
Tzanck smearMultinucleated giant cells
HistopathologyCMV owl's-eye and tissue-specific disease confirmation
Tzanck trap: multinucleated giant cells support HSV/VZV, but they do not distinguish HSV-1 from HSV-2 from VZV. PCR gives etiologic identification.

Slides 12-23: Herpes Simplex Virus 1 & 2

Slide 13. Lesion evolution shown visually: papule → vesicle → pustule → crusted ulcer.
HSV-1HSV-2
Primary infection often childhood; saliva transmission; gingivostomatitis in children or exudative pharyngitis in adultsPainful grouped genital vesicles on erythematous base, progressing to pustules/ulcers
Latency usually trigeminal ganglion in current deckRecurrent genital disease; prolonged asymptomatic shedding may occur
Herpetic whitlow, herpes gladiatorum, keratitis, encephalitis, eczema herpeticumFirst episode may include fever, adenopathy, myalgia, headache, aseptic meningitis
Slide 14. Primary HSV-1: painful oral lesions / gingivostomatitis, then latency in sensory ganglia, usually trigeminal.
Slide 16. Recurrent HSV-1 travels from latent neural site back to skin. Triggers include fever, stress, sun, trauma, decreased immunity, and steroids.
Slide 17. HSV-2 clinical manifestations: painful grouped vesicles, genital/urethral/anal disease, systemic symptoms in first episode, and asymptomatic shedding.
Slide 20. Current deck treatment: acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir for initial episodes, recurrences, and suppression.

HSV encephalitis: must-not-miss vignette

Slide 21. HSV-1 encephalitis: temporal-lobe predilection, fever/headache/behavior change/seizures, mixed CSF pleocytosis with elevated protein and RBCs, diagnosis by CSF HSV PCR, IV acyclovir.
HSV encephalitis
Temporal lobe + behavior/seizures + RBCs in CSF → HSV-1 until proven otherwise → CSF HSV PCR + IV acyclovir.
Slide 22. Additional complications include neonatal herpes, ocular keratitis/retinitis, and reactivation with esophagitis or organ disease in immunocompromised hosts.
Slide 23. Eczema herpeticum: HSV occurring in the setting of active atopic dermatitis/eczema.
Handout-only enrichment: HSV-1 classically travels by retrograde axonal transport to the trigeminal ganglion, HSV-2 to sacral ganglia; HSV keratitis produces branching dendritic ulcers. The handout also adds erythema multiforme as a possible HSV-triggered hypersensitivity reaction.

Slides 24-33: Varicella-Zoster Virus

One virus, two diseases
Primary VZV = varicella/chickenpox. Reactivation = zoster/shingles.
Slide 24. Primary varicella is chickenpox; reactivation produces dermatomal zoster. Immunocompromised patients can develop disseminated disease.
Slide 25. Chickenpox: respiratory/contact transmission, 10-14 day incubation, rash in crops from cyclic viremia, lesions in multiple stages, contagious until all crusted.
Slide 26. Healthy child with chickenpox - the deck visually reinforces lesions in different stages.
Slide 27. Disseminated varicella in an immunocompromised adult.
Slide 29. Shingles: reactivation from sensory ganglion, painful dysesthesia followed by dermatomal vesicular rash; thoracic/lumbar dermatomes are common.
Slide 31. Post-herpetic neuralgia = persistent dermatomal pain after rash resolution; the deck calls it the most common late complication.
SituationCurrent-deck management / prevention
Varicella high-risk exposureVZIG
Varicella vaccineVARIVAX for childhood prevention and susceptible adults
ZosterFamciclovir or valacyclovir; IV acyclovir if immunocompromised; start within 3 days
Shingles preventionShingrix recombinant subunit vaccine, 2 doses; healthy adults >50 and immunocompromised adults >18 per lecture
Slide 33. Shingrix: recombinant subunit vaccine with adjuvant; two-dose series; lecture recommendation includes healthy adults >50 and immunocompromised adults >18.
Handout-only enrichment: the 2029 handout emphasizes dorsal-root ganglion latency, shingles typically not crossing the midline, and herpes zoster ophthalmicus with Hutchinson sign as an emergency. Those details are useful board enrichment but are not all written on the current deck.

Slides 34-41: Epstein-Barr Virus

Slide 34. EBV disease spectrum in the current deck: infectious mononucleosis, Burkitt lymphoma, other immunodeficiency-associated lymphomas, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, post-transplant lymphoproliferative syndromes, and oral hairy leukoplakia.
Slide 37. Mono: fatigue/malaise, sore throat, fever, pharyngitis with palatal petechiae, adenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and aminopenicillin-associated rash.
Slide 39. Laboratory diagnosis: mild leukocytosis, atypical lymphocytosis (>10%) consisting of CD8 T cells, positive heterophile antibody/Monospot, and acute VCA/EA IgM patterns.
Slide 40. Peripheral smear image of atypical/reactive lymphocytes in infectious mononucleosis.
EBV mono
Fever + pharyngitis + adenopathy + splenomegaly + heterophile positive + atypical CD8 T cells.
Management: rest and no contact sports. The deck states that no specific antiviral therapy is beneficial; steroids may be used for selected serious complications such as hemolytic anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, impending airway obstruction, or CNS/cardiac disease.
Handout-only enrichment: EBV binds CD21 on B cells; the atypical “Downey cells” are reactive CD8 T cells, not infected B cells. The handout also emphasizes posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and the heterophile antibody's agglutination principle.

Slides 42-49: Cytomegalovirus

Slide 42. CMV transmission occurs through close contact with infected secretions; major primary syndromes are CMV mononucleosis, congenital CMV, and opportunistic disease in immunosuppressed hosts.
Slide 43. CMV mononucleosis in healthy young adults can mimic EBV mono but is heterophile/Monospot negative.
Slide 44. Congenital CMV / TORCH pattern in the current deck includes jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, microcephaly, cerebral calcification, chorioretinitis, and seizures.
Slide 45. Opportunistic CMV: HIV, transplant, BMT, chemotherapy; organ disease includes retinitis, pneumonitis, encephalitis, esophagitis, colitis, and neurologic disease.
Slide 46. The deck visually shows CMV retinitis, colitis, esophagitis, pneumonitis, and interstitial pneumonia.
Slide 48. Characteristic CMV owl's-eye inclusion on histopathology.
Slide 49. Current-deck treatment list: ganciclovir, valganciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir, CMV immune globulin, letermovir for prevention in BMT, maribavir for resistant CMV; no vaccine.

EBV vs CMV mononucleosis

FeatureEBVCMV
Heterophile / MonospotPositiveNegative
Atypical lymphocytesYesYes
Pharyngitis / marked adenopathyProminent in deckCan occur, but deck emphasizes mono-like mimic
Special hostTeen/young adult classic IMCongenital disease; severe opportunistic disease in transplant/HIV
Ozzy checkpoint - click him once you can separate EBV mono from CMV mono and then pivot to the correct confirmatory test.
Handout-only enrichment: congenital CMV board clues include sensorineural hearing loss and periventricular calcifications; CMV retinitis may have a “pizza-pie / ketchup-and-mustard” appearance. The handout also adds ganciclovir marrow suppression and foscarnet/cidofovir nephrotoxicity - mechanisms/toxicities are not detailed on the current deck.

Slides 50-54: HHV-6, HHV-7, HHV-8

Slide 51. HHV-6B roseola: abrupt high fever followed by defervescence and maculopapular rash; febrile seizures/encephalitis are rare neurologic complications.
Slide 52. Roseola image - rash after the fever breaks is the key sequence.
Roseola
High fever first → fever resolves → rash appears.

HHV-7: acquired in childhood, saliva transmission, syndromes similar to HHV-6; can reactivate in BMT/SOT.

Slide 54. HHV-8/KSHV: Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, and multicentric Castleman disease are the current-deck associations.
Handout-only enrichment: HHV-8 drives endothelial proliferation and angiogenesis in Kaposi sarcoma; the handout describes violaceous mucocutaneous lesions and AIDS association.

Slides 55-62: Faculty Questions = Exam Logic

Slide 55. Question 1: acute fever/headache/confusion + RBC-rich CSF + temporal-lobe inflammation. The intended confirmation is CSF HSV-1 PCR.
CSF / clinical patternInterpretation from this lecture
Temporal lobe + behavior change/seizures + RBCs + ↑proteinHSV-1 encephalitis → CSF HSV PCR
Teen + sore throat + adenopathy + positive heterophile testEBV IM → excess reactive T lymphocytes
Painful genital vesicles improving with acyclovirHSV recurrence remains possible, often less severe
Which herpesvirus illness is vaccine-preventable?Acute varicella
Slide 57. Question 2 reinforces that atypical lymphocytes in EBV mononucleosis are T lymphocytes, not B lymphocytes.
Slide 59. Question 3 reinforces latency/recurrence counseling after genital herpes.
Slide 61. Question 4 reinforces that acute varicella is vaccine-preventable.

Slides 63-66: Brief Mpox Overview

Slide 63. Mpox is an orthopoxvirus, not a herpesvirus. Current deck emphasizes direct skin-to-skin transmission from lesions, often genital in U.S. cases, ~1 week incubation, flu-like prodrome, and painful vesicles progressing to crust.
Slide 64. CDC visual examples of Mpox lesions included in the deck.
Slide 66. Current 2026 deck: diagnosis by lesion PCR; JYNNEOS is a non-replicating modified vaccinia vaccine, 2-dose IM/ID series, used for people exposed or at risk.
Important source conflict: the older MCG 2029 handout says tecovirimat can be used for severe Mpox. The current 2026 Newman-Whitlow deck explicitly says there is no known therapy and that tecovirimat failed in Mpox trials. This companion follows the current deck.

High-Yield Traps & Vignette Recognition

If you see...Think...
Temporal-lobe encephalitis + RBCs in CSFHSV-1 → CSF PCR + IV acyclovir
Painful grouped genital vesicles + recurrenceHSV-2 / genital HSV
Multiple lesion stages in cropsVaricella
Unilateral dermatomal painful vesiclesZoster
Persistent pain after zoster rash resolvesPost-herpetic neuralgia
Teen mono + heterophile positive + atypical T cellsEBV
Mono-like illness + heterophile negativeCMV
Transplant/HIV + retinitis/colitis/esophagitis + owl's eyeCMV opportunistic disease
High fever that resolves before rashHHV-6/7 roseola
Kaposi / PEL / multicentric CastlemanHHV-8
Painful inoculation-site lesions + skin-to-skin exposureMpox → lesion PCR
Last 60 seconds
HSV = neurotropic recurrence. VZV = chickenpox then shingles. EBV = heterophile-positive mono. CMV = heterophile-negative mono + congenital/opportunistic disease. HHV-6/7 = fever then rash. HHV-8 = Kaposi. Mpox is orthopox, not herpes.
